extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematics educators, mathematicians, and researchers studying mathematical explanation and proof comprehension
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principled guidance for judging when a mathematical proof is explanatory (i.e., generates understanding) for particular readers; ties accounts of explanatoriness to cognitive architecture and pedagogical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct attention / select info from sensory to working memory
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof "would have features that make it easy, or at least as easy as possible, to select the information from sensory memory into working memory that is necessary for a successful processing stage" — in other words, it effectively directs the reader’s attention to its conceptually important sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design proofs so salient, relevant information is signalled (e.g., clear structure, highlighting key steps, explicit cues). Anti-pattern: proofs that bury the key idea among lengthy technical manipulations so readers cannot easily identify the conceptually important parts. Example: proofs that use explicit signalling effects (Mautone and Mayer) help readers select relevant schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate integration with existing long-term schemas
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof "would have features that make it easier to coordinate the new knowledge contained in the proof with existing schemas retrieved from long-term memory, and therefore to reorganise the new and existing information into coherent new schemas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include references, analogies, or structuring devices that map new content onto familiar schemas. Example: invoking characterising properties or familiar definitions so readers can retrieve and integrate relevant prior knowledge. Anti-pattern: introducing entirely novel concepts without mapping to prior knowledge, which impedes schema reorganisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split working memory load across visual and verbal/auditory channels
rubrics_metrics.description: A good explanatory proof should "split the working memory load it gives to its readers between their visual and verbal/auditory channels so that the chances of their working memory capacity being exceeded ... is minimised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complementary visual representations and textual explanation to reduce cognitive load (dual-channel processing). Example: diagrams plus explanatory text. Anti-pattern: long, dense prose with no visual aids or purely visual proofs lacking any text (the latter may be less explanatory than equivalent proof with text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterising property (Steiner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs "make reference to some characterising property of an entity mentioned in the theorem" which serves as a cue to retrieve and integrate relevant schemas from long-term memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, connect the theorem and proof via an explicit characterising property so it functions as a retrieval cue and signals how to integrate knowledge. Note: if the reader lacks any existing schema for that property, the cue will not help (so explanatoriness is audience-dependent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience / symmetry linking setup, statement, and proof (Lange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs exhibiting salience (often symmetry) that "links the problem set-up, the statement of the result, and the proof itself" will make salient information easier to select and integrate, aiding understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for structural/salient alignments between hypothesis, statement, and proof steps (symmetries, recurring motifs). This acts as a signalling mechanism to guide attention and retrieval. Anti-pattern: disjoint or ad-hoc proof structure with no evident linking pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification (Kitcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs "unify phenomena by showing that they are all derivable by stringent arguments of the same form" — cognitive unification integrates multiple schemas into a single, denser schema closer to maximal understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that show common structure across cases or derive multiple results from a single principle. Scoring note: greater unificatory power typically yields greater explanatoriness for readers with relevant prior schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on unfamiliar/contradictory hypothetical worlds (limits of proofs by contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many proofs by contradiction are unlikely to generate much understanding because they involve reasoning about logically inconsistent mathematical worlds for which readers lack coherent schemas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using indirect/contradictory reasoning as the primary explanatory device; if used, ensure the argument draws directly on familiar schemas (e.g., the example that 2 is the only even prime uses familiar schemas for 'even' and 'prime'). Anti-pattern: contradiction proofs that invoke highly unfamiliar inconsistent constructs that impede schema formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce useful representational shifts / new perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs can produce understanding by presenting a productive change of perspective or representation (e.g., viewing numbers as fixed-length strings rather than magnitudes), thereby connecting previously disjoint schemas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly motivate and demonstrate the representational shift and how it connects to known techniques (e.g., combinatorics). Example: proof 3.2's shift to five-digit strings creates links to combinatoric schemas and thereby generates understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine visuals with descriptive text (visual + text > purely visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence and the account predict that visual proofs usually help because they split processing across channels, but purely visual proofs ("purely visual proofs—those that contain no text of any kind") may be less explanatory than equivalent proofs that include textual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using visuals, accompany them with descriptive text that clarifies or signals the intended interpretation. Example: adding descriptive captions to a diagram increases perceived persuasiveness and explanatory value (Inglis & Mejía-Ramos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate objectual understanding (not merely propositional knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the functional account, a proof is explanatory if it "brings about understanding" for the reader — specifically objectual understanding (understanding-how/why), rather than merely knowing that a theorem is true (propositional knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proofs by the extent they change the reader's organisation of concepts and problem-solving repertoire, not merely by whether they establish truth. Scoring note: explanatoriness is continuous — measure the degree to which objectual understanding increases relative to a contextual threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual / audience sensitivity and modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness is located at the conjunction of the reader and the proof: "A proof is explanatory for a given reader if it brings about understanding for that reader." This makes explanatoriness context dependent on the reader's prior knowledge and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or choosing a proof, model the target audience's prior schemas, working memory capacity, and instructional aims. Instructors often judge explanatoriness relative to a hypothetical audience. Anti-pattern: assuming a single proof is universally explanatory without regard to audience differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use retrieval cues / signalling effects to access long-term memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrieving information from long-term memory is facilitated in the presence of a cue that references that information (e.g., Tulving & Pearlstone); proofs should include elements that function as such cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate explicit references to familiar concepts, labels, or properties that will act as retrieval cues. Example: referencing the same characterising mathematical property in theorem and proof helps link schemas and guide integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage working memory load (chunking, scaffolding, dual-channel design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because working memory has severe capacity and temporal limits, explanatory proofs should be designed to avoid exceeding readers' working memory resources (e.g., chunking information, using diagrams plus text, rehearsable steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cognitive load principles: break proofs into manageable sub-steps, use worked examples, provide scaffolding, and split information across modalities. Empirical suggestion: secondary-task manipulations show explanatoriness ratings fall when working memory is taxed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage active processing / self-explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature (self-explanation effect) indicates that prompts or structures that encourage readers to generate explanations themselves improve understanding and thus explanatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include opportunities for the reader to self-explain (questions, prompts, minimal hints) or design proofs so readers must rephrase key steps. Anti-pattern: passive presentation with no encouragement of active integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contextual thresholds to make discrete explanatory judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Although explanatoriness is continuous, one can use contextual thresholds (per Kelp 2016) to make discrete judgments like 'this proof is explanatory, that proof is not' by assessing whether the increase in objectual understanding meets the contextually required level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether to label a proof explanatory, specify the audience and the threshold of understanding required in that context (e.g., introductory class vs expert seminar) and evaluate the proof's expected contribution relative to that threshold.
